findings.description: Across the three training-platform test splits, Brackenridge-Tox achieved higher average macro-F1 than Owlery-Enc (81.9% versus 79.8%; a 2.1-point difference), with the paired seed-level comparison statistically significant (t=10.64, p<0.001, 95% CI [1.58, 2.69]).
Brackenridge-Tox outperformed Owlery-Enc on each individual training-platform test split: Gildcrest Forums, Nettlebank, and Pikestaff Chat.
In the pooled training-platform subtype analysis, Brackenridge-Tox exceeded Owlery-Enc for all four toxicity subtypes, with the largest advantage for identity attacks (3.7 points).

The Cobble-Board result does not establish generalization to a genuinely unseen test platform because that collection was used for early stopping, checkpoint selection, and threshold choice and had no separate test partition; moreover, no significance test is reported for its model comparison.

No genuinely held-out unseen-platform test exists: the only out-of-pool evaluation (Cobble-Board) was tuned on, so the generalization question remains unanswered; the advantage is confirmed only on held-out splits of training platforms.

findings.description: Under matched Coldharbour-LiDAR timing conditions, Gossamer-Seg had substantially lower median per-scan latency than Tumbril-3D (29.4 versus 47.8 ms).
Gossamer-Seg also achieved higher matched-condition throughput (34.0 versus 20.9 scans/s) and lower 90th-percentile latency (33.1 versus 52.6 ms) than Tumbril-3D.

The speed advantage did not incur a lower mean test mIoU: Gossamer-Seg scored 67.9% versus 67.5% for Tumbril-3D, but the 0.4-percentage-point paired difference was not statistically significant (p=0.18; 95% CI −0.46 to 1.26; n=3 seeds).
Selected per-class test IoUs were mixed: Gossamer-Seg was higher for car, cyclist, and pole, but lower for pedestrian and vegetation.
Despite being faster in matched timing, Gossamer-Seg had higher analytical compute proxies than Tumbril-3D—96.3 versus 81.5 GFLOPs per scan and 41.7 versus 38.2 million parameters.

The originally published latencies are not a controlled head-to-head comparison because the methods used different accelerators, batch sizes, precision, and latency accounting, so the matched re-timing is the appropriate basis for the speed conclusion.

findings.description: Loamwise-ViT achieved higher clean Harrowfield-Leaf top-1 accuracy than Ferncastle-CNN (91.4% versus 89.7%), with a statistically significant paired mean advantage of 1.7 percentage points across five seeds.
Loamwise-ViT met the pre-specified robustness criterion at every tested JPEG quality from 90 through 10 because its accuracy drop never exceeded 1.8 points, below the 2.0-point limit.
Ferncastle-CNN met the robustness criterion only at JPEG qualities 90 and 70 and exceeded the 2.0-point drop limit at qualities 50, 30 and 10.
Under the most severe tested compression, JPEG quality 10, Loamwise-ViT retained 89.6% accuracy with a 1.8-point drop, whereas Ferncastle-CNN fell to 79.9% with a 9.8-point drop.
The JPEG evidence is limited to mean performance on one test split at five specified quality settings, and the package reports no inferential test or uncertainty interval for the JPEG comparisons.

Loamwise-ViT's JPEG robustness does not generalize to all perturbations: it exceeded the 2.0-point criterion under motion blur at 7 px (2.9) and 11 px (6.1) and under brightness ×0.6 (wait 1.7 meets) and ×0.4 (3.4). Robustness is specific to JPEG, although it still dropped less than Ferncastle-CNN.

findings.description: Across the five benchmarks, Sprocket-AD achieved a higher mean event-F1 than Lanyard-TS (78.4% versus 77.2%), a 1.2-percentage-point descriptive advantage.
Sprocket-AD had higher event-F1 than Lanyard-TS on Rookhaven-Server, Mallowmere-Water, Tinderbox-HVAC, and Whitlow-Rail, while the methods tied at 78.4% on Quayside-Grid v2.

Because no statistical tests were reported, the package establishes only a descriptive event-F1 advantage and does not establish whether Sprocket-AD's advantage over Lanyard-TS is statistically significant.
Sprocket-AD also outperformed the deterministic Dunmore-Iso baseline on every benchmark and by 13.7 percentage points in average event-F1.

Detection-delay results were mixed: relative to Lanyard-TS, Sprocket-AD had lower median delay on Rookhaven-Server, Quayside-Grid v2, and Whitlow-Rail but higher delay on Mallowmere-Water and Tinderbox-HVAC.
The full Sprocket-AD had higher average event-F1 than every ablated variant, with removing both the frequency branch and adaptive thresholds reducing the average from 78.4% to 75.8%.
The default 128-step input window produced the highest average event-F1 among the tested window lengths, although the 256-step result was close (78.4% versus 78.1%).
Compared with Lanyard-TS, Sprocket-AD used fewer parameters and had lower training and inference times (3.2 M versus 5.8 M parameters, 14 versus 22 minutes, and 0.9 versus 1.4 ms per window).
Quayside-Grid v2 uses revised labels, so its scores are not directly comparable to version 1 results; the tie there should be interpreted cautiously.

findings.description: On Fenmoor-Test across the four English→X pairs, adding pivot-filtered back-translation to Wickersham-MT increased average BLEU from 12.0 to 15.1, a gain of 3.1 points.
Wickersham-MT's 3.1-point average BLEU gain was 2.7 points smaller than the 5.8-point average improvement previously reported by Rasmussen-Obi and Petrakis (2023).
Pivot-filtered back-translation improved Wickersham-MT BLEU over genuine-only training for every evaluated pair, with gains of 3.1 for en→ne, 2.4 for en→si, 4.0 for en→km, and 2.9 for en→ps.
The improvement was also present in chrF, whose four-pair average rose from 39.0 with genuine data only to 42.3 with pivot-filtered back-translation.
Pivot filtering outperformed unfiltered back-translation by 1.7 average BLEU points and 2.0 average chrF points on Fenmoor-Test.
The comparisons are descriptive because each configuration was trained only once and no statistical tests were reported.

The roughly 6 BLEU gain attributed to Ambergate & Toivonen (2022) is not supported by their cited passage P1, which states no gain. The usable baseline is P2's 5.8 BLEU, so the comparison rests on P2, not the often-cited figure.

The previously reported gain for unfiltered back-translation was 2.9 BLEU (P2). Wickersham-MT's unfiltered gain was 1.4 (13.4 vs 12.0). Both the filtered and unfiltered gains are smaller than previously reported.

findings.description: On the Merriwold-Dialog 2.0 test set, Corvane-DST had a higher mean joint goal accuracy than Halloway-DST across five paired random seeds (56.8% versus 56.1%), an observed advantage of 0.7 percentage points.

The package reports no statistical significance test or confidence interval for the headline Corvane-DST versus Halloway-DST comparison on Merriwold-Dialog 2.0, so the 0.7-point observed advantage cannot be characterized as statistically significant from the supplied evidence.

Corvane-DST substantially outperformed the lighter Pipkin-Span baseline in Merriwold-Dialog 2.0 JGA (56.8% versus 52.3%), with a statistically significant paired mean difference of 4.5 percentage points.

On the Tarnby-Schema test set containing services unseen during training, Corvane-DST exceeded Halloway-DST in mean JGA by 2.3 percentage points (41.9% versus 39.6%), and the paired test supported this advantage.
The single-domain Merriwold-Dialog 2.0 results were mixed: Corvane-DST exceeded Halloway-DST for train, restaurant, and attraction dialogues but trailed it for hotel and taxi dialogues.

Corvane-DST's advantage over Halloway-DST is small on the in-domain test set (0.7 points, with overlapping SDs of 0.6 and 1.3). It is larger on unseen-service Tarnby-Schema (2.3 points, significant). Per-domain results are mixed, so the benefit is not uniform.

findings.description: On the standard shaped-reward Thistlewood-Manip suite, Heronsgate achieved 64.3% average success versus Pallister's 61.8%, an advantage of 2.5 percentage points.

The 2.5-percentage-point shaped-reward advantage of Heronsgate over Pallister was statistically significant in the paired eight-seed comparison (two-sided paired t-test, p=0.0015; 95% CI [1.33, 3.67]).
Heronsgate's per-task shaped-reward results were mixed: it outperformed Pallister on drawer-open, block-stack, door-unlock, and lid-twist, but underperformed on peg-insert and cable-route.

On the secondary sparse-reward suite, Heronsgate's observed average-success advantage over Pallister was only 0.7 percentage points and was not statistically significant (p=0.47), so the shaped-reward superiority did not carry over conclusively to this setting.
Heronsgate required more training compute than Pallister on the main evaluation, using 9.5 versus 7.8 GPU-hours.

findings.description: On the six scaffold-split test sets, Larchmont-GNN achieved higher mean test ROC-AUC than Quintrell-MP on every dataset, with dataset-level gains ranging from 0.3 to 1.6 ROC-AUC points.
Averaged across the six datasets, Larchmont-GNN scored 79.4 versus 78.4 for Quintrell-MP, an advantage of 1.0 ROC-AUC point.
Larchmont-GNN did not surpass the pretrained Avonlea-Chem-XL overall: its average was 0.6 points lower, although it scored higher on Hollin-Sol and Jessamine-Kin and lower on the other four datasets.

The ablation results support contributions from both added components: removing ring-aware pooling, distance features, or both reduced the six-dataset average from 79.4 to 78.7, 78.9, and 78.0, respectively.
Because no statistical tests were reported, the package does not establish whether Larchmont-GNN's observed advantages over Quintrell-MP are statistically significant.

Larchmont-GNN costs slightly more than Quintrell-MP (4.8M vs 4.1M parameters; 210 vs 180 ms per 1,000 molecules). Neither needs pretraining. Avonlea-Chem-XL is far larger and costlier (310M parameters, 2950 ms, 2400 GPU-hours), and Larchmont-GNN's average is within 0.6 points of it.
